newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jewish settlers in Hebron mourn Israeli handover.
newsitem.headline: Jewish settlers in Hebron mourn Israeli handover.

text.p: Jewish settlers tore their clothes and prayed on Friday to mourn Israel's handover of most of Hebron to Palestinian rule after 30 years of occupation.
"It is a very sad day, a day of mourning," said Noam Arnon, spokesman for the 400 settlers who live in the heart of 100,000 Arabs. "We tear our clothes and pray to mourn for what has happened."
Like Palestinians, settlers said they feared for their safety. The town is a flashpoint of Arab-Jewish violence.

Arnon and 30 other men in religious skullcaps gathered near Hebron's ancient Jewish cemetery overlooking the city. Each one cut a small hole in his shirt just below the collar and then tore the shirt. All read from the biblical Book of Psalms.
Jews traditionally tear their clothes when mourning the death of a relative.

Hours earlier Israel vacated its military headquarters overlooking the town and Palestinian policemen moved in to the sound of sirens and firecrackers. Five soldiers for each settler remained to guard the Jews in the fifth of the town that stays under Israeli control.

Settlers, believing Hebron to be their biblical birthright, opposed the U.S.-brokered accord to hand over parts of the town. They believe that Abraham, father of the Jews, is buried there in the Cave of Machpelah described in the Bible.

"The people should not give away their homeland and this is a very important part of our homeland," Arnon said, adding: "It's not a victory of justice or liberation. It is a day of cruelty and injust occupation."
Most Israelis favoured the pullback. More than 70 percent of Israel's parliament backed the deal.

According to a Gallup poll of 509 Jewish Israelis published in the newspaper Maariv on Friday, 57 percent favour the Hebron deal while 19 percent oppose it, 19 percent are undecided and 5 percent have no response.

Israel poured troop and police reinforcements into Hebron to prevent protests by Jewish settlers opposed to the handover. An Israeli general issued orders on Thursday restricting the movements of 18 alleged Jewish militants for up to 10 days.
"It is a very dangerous step for the security of the state of Israel. I am concerned about my safety," Arnon said.
"The conditions have now been created to cause riots and violent demonstrations which could lead to attacks against Jews in the city," he told Reuters.
In 1929 Arab rioters, opposed to rising Jewish immigration and inflamed by sermons at local mosques, massacred 67 men, women and children in the town, then home to some 700 Jews.
But settlers were not the only ones to fear attacks.
In February 1994, settler Baruch Goldstein of the nearby Kiryat Arba settlement massacred 29 Palestinians kneeling in prayer at al-Ibrahimi mosque before survivors beat him to death.
The fate of the Jews in Hebron and in other West Bank settlements will be decided in "final-status" talks between Israel and the Palestinians due to be completed by May 1999.
